surah.tagline: Four verses that say who God is, and who He is not.
surah.status: Draft · items marked verify need scholar review

theme.text: The surah is a complete statement of tawḥīd: who God is (One, al-Ṣamad) and what He is not (not begetting, not begotten, without equal).
theme.source: General tafsir: al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī on 112

theme.text: The Prophet ﷺ said that this surah equals a third of the Qurʾān.
theme.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5013, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī

theme.text: Scholars explain the "third" in different ways. One common explanation: the Qurʾān's content falls into rulings, narratives, and the description of God, and this surah gathers the third kind.
theme.scholar: Reported in al-Qurṭubī among other explanations

miracle.title: One rhyme, one Lord
miracle.text: All four verses end on the sound -ad: aḥad, ṣamad, yūlad, aḥad. The final dāl is a qalqala letter, which ends each verse with a short, firm stop.

miracle.title: Each verse sealed
miracle.text: Because every verse lands on a closed, firm sound, each statement about God feels complete and final when recited. Nothing trails off.

miracle.title: Fifteen words
miracle.text: In fifteen Arabic words the surah affirms two things (He is One, He is al-Ṣamad) and denies three (begetting, being begotten, having any equal). Nothing is repeated except the name Allāh and the word aḥad.

miracle.title: Opens and closes with aḥad
miracle.text: The surah's statement begins with aḥad (verse 1) and ends with aḥad (verse 4). The first affirms that He is One; the last denies that anyone is like Him.

revelation.text: Most scholars count the surah as Makkan; others count it as Madinan. The difference follows the reports about who asked the question that it answers (see verse 1).
revelation.scholar: Both positions are discussed by Ibn ʿĀshūr
revelation.source: Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr, introduction to 112

claims.text: al-Masad names a man by his kunya, Abū Lahab, and says his wealth and what he earned will not save him. al-Ikhlāṣ follows with the One who has no lineage and needs nothing. Human lineage and wealth fail; God is beyond both.
al-Ikhlāṣ, al-Falaq and al-Nās all open with "qul" (say). The Prophet ﷺ would recite the three together before sleeping.
claims.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Book of the Virtues of the Qurʾān, from ʿĀʾisha

claims.text: al-Ikhlāṣ first establishes who God is; al-Falaq and al-Nās then seek refuge in Him. Knowing the One comes before asking Him for protection.

claim.text: No ring structure is claimed. Four short verses are too few to establish one; the aḥad framing is noted above as a reflection.

meanings: to state a view or belief

why.text: Imperative form. The command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to everyone who recites it.

words.lexSource: al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt, entry q-w-l; Lane's Lexicon, q-w-l

translations.text: The truth is / The matter is

why.text: The pronoun can point back to the one asked about, or it can be the pronoun of the matter, which announces that a weighty statement follows.
Scholars differ on whether the name is derived (from ilāh, "the one who is worshipped") or is a proper name with no derivation. Both views are old, and this study does not choose between them.
why.scholar: al-Rāghib discusses the derivation; the disagreement is reported among grammarians

special.text: A proper name used only for the one true God. Grammarians note that it takes no plural and no dual.

why.text: In an affirmative sentence, aḥad in this absolute sense is used only of God. Elsewhere it mostly comes after a negation, meaning "anyone".

special.text: When Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ was tortured in Makkah to make him give up Islam, he kept repeating one word: "Aḥad, aḥad."
special.scholar: Ibn Isḥāq's Sīra, as transmitted by Ibn Hishām

words.lexSource: al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt, entry aḥad; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, w-ḥ-d

layers.reading: "He" is the Lord they asked about
layers.translation: Say: He is Allah, the One.
layers.note: The answer to their question: the Lord you ask about is Allah.

explanation.text: People asked about the Prophet's Lord. The pronoun huwa points back to the One they asked about, and the answer names Him.

tafsir.text: Say, O Muhammad, to those who asked you about your Lord: He is Allah, One.
He is the One, the Unique, with no peer, no helper, no rival, no likeness and no equal.

layers.translation: Say: The truth is this: Allah is One.
layers.note: The pronoun works like a pause before a great truth.

explanation.text: huwa can be ḍamīr al-shaʾn, the "pronoun of the matter". Arabic uses it to draw attention before a statement of great weight, like saying "Here is the truth:".

tafsir.text: Mentions this reading alongside the first: the pronoun stands for "the matter", and "Allāhu aḥad" is the matter it introduces.

layers.translation: Say: He is Allah, One without parts.
layers.note: Not only one in number, but one with no parts.

explanation.text: aḥad does more than count to one. It denies a second like Him, and it also denies that He is made of parts.

tafsir.text: Explains aḥad, when used of God, as the one that admits no plurality in any respect.

miracle.title: Aḥad, not wāḥid
miracle.text: Arabic has two words for one. wāḥid can begin a count (one, two, three), so it leaves room for a second. aḥad, used of God, closes that door: no second, and no division.

miracle.title: Indefinite on purpose
miracle.text: The verse says aḥadun, not al-aḥad. The indefinite suggests a oneness that belongs to no category. He is not "the one" of a known group.

miracle.title: Why "Say" stays
miracle.text: The command "qul" is kept in the recited words. The reciter repeats what they were told to say, which marks the surah as a message passed on, not something composed.

narration.text: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reported that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Describe your Lord's lineage to us," and God revealed this surah.
narration.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, Book of Tafsīr, on 112; Musnad Aḥmad

grading.text: al-Tirmidhī also gives the report without Ubayy (mursal, from Abū al-ʿĀliya) and says that version is more correct. The connected chain includes Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī, about whom the hadith critics differ. Later graders disagree on whether it is ḥasan or weak.

disagreement.text: Other reports say the question came from Jews of Madinah, not from the Quraysh. al-Ṭabarī collects reports on both sides. This is where the Makkan or Madinan disagreement comes from.

why.text: Scholars differ on whether the name is derived (from ilāh, "the one who is worshipped") or is a proper name with no derivation. Both views are old, and this study does not choose between them.
why.scholar: al-Rāghib discusses the derivation; the disagreement is reported among grammarians

special.text: A proper name used only for the one true God. Grammarians note that it takes no plural and no dual.

words.rootMeaning: to aim for; to be solid
meanings: to aim for, to turn to (qaṣd)
the master to whom people turn in their needs
the master perfect in his mastery
the one who remains, the Everlasting

why.text: Ibn Fāris gives the root two core senses: aiming for something, and solidity. The early exegetes explain al-Ṣamad with several meanings built on these, and al-Ṭabarī collects their reports. All of them are carried at once.
why.source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, ṣ-m-d; Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 112:2

special.text: In the narration of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Ṣamad is explained by the next verse: the One who does not beget and was not begotten, because everything born will die and everything that dies is inherited, and God does not die and is not inherited.
special.scholar: Narration of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, recorded by al-Tirmidhī
special.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, Book of Tafsīr, on 112

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, ṣ-m-d; Lane's Lexicon, ṣ-m-d

layers.translation: Allah is the One to whom all turn in their needs.
layers.note: Every creature, knowingly or not, turns to Him in need.

explanation.text: From the root sense of aiming for and turning to: every creature, knowingly or not, is headed toward Him in its need.

tafsir.text: Reports from early exegetes explain al-Ṣamad as the master to whom people turn when they need something.

layers.translation: Allah is the Self-Sufficient, with no hollowness and no need.
layers.note: Nothing hollow, nothing lacking. He needs nothing.

explanation.text: From the root sense of solidity: something with no hollow inside, nothing that needs filling. He neither eats nor drinks.

tafsir.text: A group of the early exegetes explained al-Ṣamad as the one who has no hollow inside.
tafsir.scholar: Reported by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr
tafsir.source: Jāmiʿ al-Bayān and Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr, on 112:2

layers.translation: Allah is the Master, perfect in His mastery.
layers.note: The one everyone relies on, without any limit.

explanation.text: A ṣamad among the Arabs was a chief whom people relied on. Applied to God, the word means a mastery with no flaw or limit.

tafsir.text: The master who is perfect in his mastery, the noble who is perfect in his nobility, perfect in knowledge, wisdom and every attribute.
tafsir.scholar: Ibn ʿAbbās (through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa), as reported by Ibn Kathīr

layers.translation: Allah is the Everlasting, who remains after His creation.
layers.note: He remains when everything else is gone.

explanation.text: The one who remains when everything else ends.

tafsir.text: al-Ṣamad is the Everlasting, who remains after His creation.
tafsir.scholar: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatāda, as reported by Ibn Kathīr

miracle.title: A word used once
miracle.text: al-Ṣamad appears only here in the whole Qurʾān. One rare word holds what English needs four words for: refuge, self-sufficient, master, everlasting.

miracle.title: Both ends definite
miracle.text: Both parts of the sentence are definite: Allāh, al-Ṣamad. In Arabic rhetoric this pattern can express exclusivity: Allah, and only Allah, is al-Ṣamad.

miracle.title: The name, repeated
miracle.text: The verse repeats the name Allāh instead of saying "He is al-Ṣamad". Each verse then stands on its own as a full statement about God by name.

miracle.title: No "and"
miracle.text: There is no "and" between verse 1 and verse 2. The second follows directly, as if it explains the first.

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.

meanings: not (negates the past; puts the verb in the jussive)

why.text: lam with the present-form verb gives a past negation: "did not".
Active voice, with God as the subject. It denies that He has a child.

special.text: This answers people who claimed God has a son (2:116, 19:88) and the Arabs who called the angels His daughters (16:57, 37:149).

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, w-l-d; Lane's Lexicon, w-l-d

why.text: wa joins the second negation to the first.

meanings: to be begotten, to be born

why.text: Passive voice of the same root. It denies that He has a parent or any origin.

special.text: Having no parent means having no beginning. Compare 57:3: "He is the First and the Last."

verses.literal: Not [has He] begotten, and not [has He] been begotten.

layers.translation: He has not begotten, and He has not been begotten.
layers.note: He has no child and no parent.

explanation.text: The plain meaning of lam with the jussive: neither of these has happened.

tafsir.text: How could He have a son when He has no companion? (6:101). The Qurʾān answers the same claim in several places.
He has no child, no parent and no consort.

layers.translation: He never begets, and He was never begotten.
layers.note: Not only in the past, but at no time at all.

explanation.text: The verse describes God's nature, so the past negation can be read as covering all time.

tafsir.text: Everything that is born will die, and everything that dies is inherited. God does not die and is not inherited.
tafsir.scholar: Narration of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, recorded by al-Tirmidhī
tafsir.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, Book of Tafsīr, on 112

miracle.title: Begetting comes first
miracle.text: "Has not begotten" comes before "has not been begotten". People had claimed that God has children; nobody claimed that He was born. The verse answers the claim that was actually made first.
miracle.source: A common explanation in tafsir; a named source is still needed

miracle.title: One root, two directions
miracle.text: The same root in two voices: yalid (begets) and yūlad (is begotten). Together they close off both directions: no descendants, no ancestors.

miracle.title: Perfect balance
miracle.text: Two halves of equal length and pattern: lam yalid / wa-lam yūlad. The balance itself sounds like a closed matter.

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.

why.text: Past negation, joined to the previous verse.
kāna works here as a linking verb. Its subject is aḥad and its predicate is kufuwan.
li (for, to) with the pronoun hu (Him).

meanings: a peer in rank or standing

why.text: kufuʾ is a match or peer: someone of the same standing.

special.text: The same word family gives kafāʾa, the term in Islamic law for two spouses being suitable matches in standing. The verse denies that anyone is God's "match" in that sense.

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, k-f-ʾ; Lane's Lexicon, k-f-ʾ

why.text: After a negation, aḥad covers every possible individual: no one at all.

verses.literal: And not has been for Him [an] equal, [any] one.

layers.translation: And there has never been anyone equal to Him.
layers.note: Nothing and no one stands level with Him.

explanation.text: The usual parsing: the predicate kufuwan is placed before the subject aḥad.

tafsir.text: There is nothing like Him (42:11). No one shares His essence, attributes or actions.
He has no equal, no likeness and no rival.

layers.reading: No one stands toward Him as an equal
layers.translation: And no one has ever stood toward Him as an equal.
layers.note: A second way to read the grammar, still being checked.

explanation.text: Some grammarians allow kufuwan as a ḥāl (a word describing a state). Confirm the source before keeping this layer.
explanation.scholar: Reported in works of iʿrāb, possibly al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī, al-Durr al-Maṣūn

miracle.title: "To Him", placed first
miracle.text: lahu (to Him) comes before kufuwan (an equal), although such a phrase would normally come later. It is moved forward because the point is to deny an equal to God specifically.

miracle.title: Kufuw, not mithl
miracle.text: The verse uses kufuw (an equal in rank), not mithl (a likeness) or nidd (a rival). So it denies anyone who could stand at God's level, not only anyone who looks like Him.

miracle.title: The final aḥad
miracle.text: The surah ends on the same word that ended its first verse. In verse 1 aḥad means "One"; here, after a negation, it means "anyone". The same word affirms His oneness and denies every rival.

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.
